summary: This informational memo describes misbehaviour of some authoritative DNS servers when queried for AAAA records, which hold IPv6 addresses. Such behaviour can block IPv4 communication that should work, cause delays in name resolution, or contribute to denial of service. It documents the problems in detail.

plainLanguage.summary: Some DNS servers get confused when asked for the new style of address and give wrong or no answers. This document lists how they misbehave so people can fix them.

questions: dns servers misbehaving for ipv6 records
what should a dns server return for a missing aaaa record
subtitle: How some DNS servers answer IPv6 address queries wrongly, and why that can break IPv4 connections.

tldr.problem: IPv6-capable resolvers ask for AAAA records first and then fall back to A records, but some authoritative servers answer AAAA queries incorrectly.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists five known misbehaviors: ignoring the query, returning Name Error, returning other error codes, returning a broken answer, and creating a lame delegation. It explains the effect of each.
tldr.outcome: The results include blocked IPv4 connectivity, long delays, wasted queries and a possible denial of service. The correct behavior is an empty answer with RCODE 0.

today: RFC 4074 is an Informational memo from June 2005, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It records misbehaviors known when it was written and says the Name Error examples known to the authors had all been fixed.

sections.title: Why AAAA Queries Matter
sections.content:
Many resolvers that support IPv6 first look up AAAA resource records (IPv6 addresses) for a host name and then look up A records (IPv4 addresses) for the same name. This fallback follows the DNS specifications. If authoritative servers do not obey them, a web browser may fail to connect to a server it could otherwise reach.

The memo assumes three components: stub resolvers, caching servers and authoritative servers. A stub resolver sends a recursive query to a caching server, which does the full resolution and caches the result. Authoritative servers answer for their own names, normally non-recursively. The authors say the misbehavior is not specific to AAAA: all known examples also apply to MX, NS and SOA queries. They focus on AAAA because IPv6-capable resolvers at end users make the problem particularly severe.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer first asks for the new kind of address, and if there is none it asks for the old kind. That only works if the answer to the first question is honest.

sections.title: The Expected Answer
sections.content:
If a server has an A record but no AAAA record for a name, it should answer an AAAA query with RCODE 0 (no error) and an empty answer section. That tells the stub resolver the name exists with at least one record of another type, so it can look for A records.

It also lets the caching server remember that this name has no AAAA record while other types may exist, which speeds up later queries.
sections.plainLanguage: The right answer is 'I have no new-style address for that name, but the name is real.' Then everyone can move on and try the old kind.

sections.title: Five Kinds of Misbehavior
sections.content:
Ignoring the query. The stub resolver waits and may hit a fatal timeout, or the user suffers a long delay, which is worst for interactive uses like web browsing.

Returning Name Error (RCODE 3). This says no records of any type exist for the name. The resolver may give up and never fall back, and the caching server caches the negative response and returns it for A queries too. The authors say all the examples known to them have been fixed.

Other error codes. RCODE 4 (Not Implemented) is less harmful because a fallback to A works. But one server returned RCODE 2 (Server failure), and a widely deployed mail server with a certain resolver library treated that as a reason to retry and never fell back, so mail delivery failed. Caching servers do not cache these errors, which causes redundant AAAA queries, wasted bandwidth and more load on the authoritative server. RCODE 1 (Format error) would have a similar effect, but the authors had not seen it.

Broken responses. Some servers return an AAAA record whose data is only 4 bytes, like an IPv4 address (the memo shows www.bad.example. 600 IN AAAA 192.0.2.1). One widely deployed caching server passes and caches it. Another replies with RCODE 2, with the redundant-query effect.

Lame delegation. The parent zone names a server as authoritative, but that server does not give an authoritative answer (the AA bit is not set) to AAAA queries while it does for A queries. The caching server treats the delegation as lame and returns RCODE 2. Some caching servers then mark the server lame for a period, so even the A fallback fails. Others still try it as a last resort, which only costs redundant AAAA queries.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad servers might stay silent, say the name does not exist, shout an error, hand back nonsense, or act like they are not in charge. Each one can leave your computer stuck or doing useless work.

sections.title: Denial of Service
sections.content: The CERT/CC pointed out that the Name Error (RCODE 3) response described above can be used for a denial of service attack. The memo says the same argument applies to lame delegation with a certain type of caching server.
sections.plainLanguage: If a server wrongly says a real name does not exist, people cannot reach that place, and a bad actor could use that on purpose.

items.label: No error
items.desc: Correct reply to an AAAA query for a name with no AAAA record, with an empty answer.

items.label: Format error
items.desc: Would have a similar effect to other error codes; not seen in implementations by the authors.

items.label: Server failure
items.desc: Seen from a server and from caching servers after bad or lame answers; may stop the fallback.

items.label: Name Error
items.desc: Says the name has no records of any type; can stop the fallback and be cached.

items.label: Not Implemented
items.desc: The server does not support the requested query type.

references.text: Mockapetris, P., "Domain names - concepts and facilities", STD 13, RFC 1034, November 1987.
